## Revisiting the three thesis questions

**Has thermal-water outflow at Steamboat changed since Sorey's own
studies?** The clearest answer this proposal can give today is "not
in kind, though perhaps somewhat in magnitude." The chloride-to-boron
signature of the real thermal end-member is statistically
distinguishable between the 1950-1991 baseline and the 2024-2026
samples (19.6 versus 21.9, p = 0.015), but the shift is small, and its
cause -- a genuine geochemical change of roughly 12%, versus a
difference in analytical method between eras separated by three
decades -- cannot be disentangled from the data on hand. The
discharge estimate is even less settled: this project's single real
paired chloride-and-discharge measurement (58.7 L/s) and its own
2026 poster's multi-date average (roughly 27 L/s) both sit within,
not clearly below, the range of discharge estimates reported across
the 1955-2026 record, and Sorey and Spielman [@sorey2017] themselves
document real seasonal variability large enough to explain much of
that spread on its own. What this proposal can rule out, at least
provisionally, is a wholesale change in source water: the conservative
Cl/B signature is essentially the same fluid three decades later, and
the two independent geothermometers (Chapter 4) diverge in exactly the
way expected for a single cooling, diluting reservoir, not two
disconnected water types. What it cannot yet answer is Sorey
[@sorey2000]'s specific open question: whether any of the same vents
that stopped flowing by 1989 and had still not resumed by 2000 are
flowing again in 2026. That is a direct, field-checkable question this
thesis's own spring-remapping survey is positioned to answer, and it
has not yet been formally cross-checked against Sorey's own named
site list.

**Can continuous conductivity substitute for discrete chloride
sampling?** The Monte Carlo result in Chapter 4 is encouraging in
principle -- reconstruction error grows smoothly and stays under about
5% for daily sampling using specific conductance's own record as a
proxy for itself -- but this is not yet a real test of whether
chloride actually tracks conductance closely at Steamboat, because no
real chloride sample yet overlaps the period the loggers have been
running. This is the single most direct, most tractable gap this
thesis can close with one field season of the calibration sampling
proposed in Chapter 6, and it should be treated as the highest
priority of the concrete next steps below.

**What does the subsurface plumbing actually look like?** This is the
least resolved of the three questions, and honestly so. It depends on
two things that do not yet exist: water-level data from wells inside
the Steamboat field itself (not the wider South Truckee Meadows basin,
which is hydrogeologically distinct), and a digitized fault geometry
to build a real three-dimensional geologic model on top of. Both are
concrete, identifiable blockers with a known path to resolving them,
laid out below, rather than open-ended unknowns.

## What the new three-month field-parameter time series implies for modeling choice

The real, roughly monthly pH/conductance/temperature record described
in Chapter 4 (14 sites, late September through December 2025) bears
directly on how the subsurface should eventually be modeled, not just
on what is observed. The stable ~1.5-2 pH-unit gap between the
injection-side ports and the shallow monitoring/domestic well network,
present in every round rather than a single snapshot, is the kind of
signal that favors a reactive-transport framing (geochemical
speciation and water-rock buffering along a flow path, which this
project's PHREEQC machinery already supports) over a purely
conservative mixing model, at least for pH specifically. Conversely,
Herz Deep's rising conductance and NDOT's falling temperature over the
same window move in directions that are not explained by each other at
the same well, which argues against treating any single field
parameter as a universal stand-in for thermal fraction across the
whole field -- a caution worth carrying into any future lumped-
parameter or box-model attempt. Neither pattern is yet a resolved
finding; both are concrete, data-grounded discussion points for
choosing a defensible next modeling step, which is why they are raised
here rather than treated as settled in Chapter 4.

## What the new fissure gas data implies, and a lesson for future sampling

The April 2026 fissure gas samples (Chapter 4) are a real, independent
line of evidence, not a redundant one: the gas-geothermometer pattern
reproduces the same above/below-measured-temperature split already
seen in the water geothermometers, strengthening the case for a single
cooling, diluting flow path rather than two unrelated water types. The
flagged sample, NV26-2, is a concrete and low-cost lesson for the
calibration field season proposed above -- future Giggenbach-bottle
sampling at this terrace should avoid breaking through fresh pavement
and should re-check bottle seals before leaving the site, rather than
discovering a contamination risk after the fact. A first real PHREEQC
gas-phase run (Chapter 4) -- equilibrating SBF_0001's water against a
gas phase seeded with NV26-1's real composition -- found a real
disequilibrium, not agreement: the modeled pH and carbonate saturation
states both shift substantially away from what the water alone
predicts. That is a genuinely useful constraint, not a dead end -- it
argues against treating this system's gas and water as a single,
always-equilibrated fluid, and motivates collecting a real time-paired
gas/water sample (rather than two days apart, as here) as a concrete
next step for this thread.


## A gas-informed parent fluid, traced to the creek: what it does and does not yet show

Extending that first gas-phase run into a full steam-loss/gas-add-back
reconstruction (Chapter 4) is the thesis's first attempt to connect a
deep, pre-boiling parent fluid all the way through measured discharge
to what this project already measures at Steamboat Creek and the
downstream conductivity logger. What it shows now: the fissure and
resort-tank parent fluids converge tightly on chloride and several
other conservative species once each is corrected back toward its own
reservoir temperature, and the three real thermal points' independently
derived sodium/potassium reservoir temperatures sit within 7 degrees
Celsius of each other -- both real, specific pieces of evidence for a
single shared deep source, not proof of one. What it does not yet
show: a time-paired gas and water sample (the same limitation already
flagged above), a converged gas-equilibration step for the resort-tank
fluid specifically (a real PHREEQC convergence failure, reported rather
than hidden), or any real digitized boundary between the terrace's
degassing and seepage zones -- the conceptual figure's framing of
discrete point-source degassing versus diffuse creek-channel seepage is
a qualitative read of imagery already in hand, offered because it is a
real, testable prediction worth stating now, not because the
underlying thermal-infrared rasters have been formally digitized (they
have not -- see the Lower Sinter Terrace mapping item above). Once
those rasters are on file, the natural next step is to turn that
qualitative read into an actual spatial layer (mirroring the
`SBO_*` photo-survey-point convention already used elsewhere in this
project) and test it directly against where the spring-remapping
fieldwork finds active discharge versus dry ground.
## The chemistry-first modeling principle, and what it implies going forward

A theme running through Chapters 2 and 3 is worth restating here
explicitly, because it will matter more, not less, once a three-
dimensional geologic model exists to tempt a shortcut: a defensible
mixing or reaction-path model should be built from which samples are
genuinely distinct, chemically credible end-members, not from which
samples happen to be close together on a map. Two locations can be
close and hydraulically unconnected, or far apart and connected
through a fracture network that a map alone would not suggest. The
real mixing model already run in this project followed this logic --
its two end-members were chosen because they are chemically distinct
(chloride concentrations of 815 and 45 mg/L), not because they are
near each other -- and the same discipline should be carried forward
once fault geometry and a Leapfrog model exist: those tools should be
used to test which chemically-plausible end-members are worth pairing,
not to define the chemistry itself.

## Concrete roadblocks and how they are sequenced

Three roadblocks currently limit how far this work can go, and they
are listed here in the order that resolving each one unblocks the
next.

1. **No real chloride sample yet overlaps the conductivity-logger
   deployment window.** This blocks the entire chloride-conductivity
   calibration objective (Chapter 4's Monte Carlo result is a
   preparatory analysis, not yet a real calibration) and blocks real,
   time-paired end-member selection for PHREEQC mixing and inverse
   modeling. It is resolved by collecting new chloride samples during
   an active logger deployment -- exactly the campaign proposed in
   Chapter 6.
2. **Too few wells inside the Steamboat field itself have current,
   usable water-level data.** This blocks a real, field-specific
   potentiometric surface and a site-specific barometric efficiency
   (Chapter 4's two real barometric-efficiency values come from wells
   outside the field, in the wider South Truckee Meadows basin, and
   should not be treated as representative of a true thermal well or
   spring). A standing data request to NDEP for daily water levels and
   pressure at several named production and monitor wells, and for
   more precise surveyed well locations, is already drafted and sent;
   receiving that data is the concrete next step.
3. **No fault trace has been digitized anywhere in this project.**
   This blocks the Leapfrog three-dimensional geologic model, any
   fault-aware regrouping of PHREEQC end-members, and any future
   groundwater-flow-model zonation. The recommended path is digitizing
   the fault-and-lineament map in Collar and Huntley [@collar1990] in
   ArcGIS, using this project's own well coordinates as control
   points; the ingestion pathway for the resulting shapefile is
   already built and waiting.

## What resolving these would make possible

Once real, temporally-paired chloride and conductance samples exist,
a genuine calibration regression (not a synthetic self-test) can be
fit, and the resulting relationship can be used to reconstruct a
continuous chloride-flux record, and by extension a continuous
discharge estimate, rather than the single-date or multi-date-average
snapshots this proposal currently reports. Once field-specific water
levels exist, a real potentiometric surface can be interpolated in
ArcGIS around the Lower Sinter Terrace, giving an independent,
non-chemical line of evidence about flow direction to compare against
the facies and mixing results in Chapter 4. Once fault geometry
exists, a real Leapfrog model can be built from well collars,
completions, and the digitized structure, letting the chemistry-first
mixing results be tested against an actual candidate geometry for the
first time, and providing the hydrostratigraphic zonation a future
groundwater flow model would need. None of these three steps depends
on the others in a way that would force a particular order beyond what
is listed above; all three can, in principle, proceed in parallel
during the coming field season.

## Longer-term directions, out of scope for this proposal

A full MODFLOW-style groundwater flow model is the natural longer-term
destination for this line of work, but it depends on the Leapfrog
model and the potentiometric surface both existing first, plus a real
recharge estimate -- for which the one real precipitation-response
signal already detected at a South Truckee Meadows monitoring well is
a start, not a calibration. Expanded PHREEQC reaction-path and gas-
geochemistry modeling (the D'Amore-Panichi gas geothermometer and
gas-mixing modules are already built and validated against published
Mariner and Janik [@mariner1995] values, but have never been run
against this project's own real gas chemistry, because no real
dissolved-gas sample yet exists) would benefit from the same
temporally-paired sampling this proposal's calibration campaign is
designed to produce. Both are named here as explicit future work, not
as part of the thesis this proposal describes.

## Closing

This proposal argues that Steamboat's thermal-water chemistry has not
changed in kind since Sorey's own studies, that a workable method for
turning continuous conductivity into a chloride proxy is close to
being testable for the first time, and that the tools needed to
finally connect this chemistry to a real subsurface geometry -- a
water-level network and a digitized fault map -- are identified,
requested, and in one case already partially built and simply waiting
for real input. The remaining work is not open-ended: it is a specific
field season of calibration sampling, a specific data request, and a
specific GIS digitizing task, each already scoped in the chapters
above.
